passage:
Dear Noor,
I haven't been to school since Wednesday. Ammi thinks I have a stomach ache. I don't.
You know the photo from the fete, me standing near those boys from the other school? Someone cropped it and wrote things under it. Now in the corridor people stop talking when I pass. Girls I've known since class one look away.
Bhaijaan saw it. He told Abbu, and Abbu said a girl from our family must not give people reasons to talk, and maybe I should stop going to tuition and come straight home. He didn't even ask me what happened. I just stood there.
I eat lunch in the library now. I don't feel like myself.
Please don't show this letter to anyone. I just needed to tell someone.
Hafsa

qa.q: Since which day has Hafsa not been to school?
qa.a: She has not been to school since Wednesday.

qa.q: How can you tell Hafsa feels alone?
qa.a: She eats lunch in the library, friends from class one look away, and her father made a decision without even asking her what happened.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's missing school signal, and what could help now?
qa.a: It is a warning sign that she needs support; Noor could gently encourage her to tell a trusted teacher or counsellor, who can help with the school and her family. 🤍

qa.q: How might Noor feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Noor would likely feel worried and sad for Hafsa, and torn between keeping the letter private and wanting to get her help.

grounding: It shows a teenage girl stared at and whispered about, facing family restrictions over her reputation, isolating herself and skipping school.

passage:
Bhavna, you asked why I stopped coming for evening walks. Okay. I'll tell you.
It started with that fake story about me and the boy from coaching. You know it isn't true. But when I walk into class, it's like the room changes temperature. People whisper, they look at my bag, my phone. Some boys even said things near the cycle stand.
Then someone told my mother's friend. Now every night Mummy says, "Minakshi, give me your phone," and checks it. Papa says girls like me, from good families, must be careful what people say. As if I did something.
Last week I pretended to be sick three days in a row. I just sat in my room.
I'm tired, Bhavna. I don't know who's on my side anymore. You're the first person I've said all this to.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's mother do every night now?
qa.a: Minakshi says her mother checks her phone every night.

qa.q: What does Minakshi mean when she says she doesn't know who's on her side?
qa.a: She feels alone and blamed, with classmates whispering and even her parents acting as if she did something wrong.

qa.q: What should Bhavna do after hearing this?
qa.a: Listen and believe her, then help her talk to a trusted teacher or school counsellor soon, since pretending to be sick to skip school is a sign things need action.

qa.q: How might Minakshi's parents be seeing the situation?
qa.a: They may be scared about what people are saying about the family, and that fear leads them to control her rather than hear her side.

grounding: It illustrates the teen target of a false rumour enduring stares, strict family pressure over girls' reputation, isolation and missed school.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Wednesday

Shreya has been absent Monday and Tuesday. When she came today, she sat alone at the back and kept her dupatta pulled close. During break, two boys whistled as she passed; several girls whispered and looked away.

I kept her back after the bell. She told me, crying, that a photo of her talking to a boy at the tuition gate had been passed around with lies attached. Her father had seen it, shouted at her and said she might not go back to school.

I told her clearly that she had done nothing wrong and that I was glad she told me. I stayed with her and took her to the counsellor's room. I phoned her mother and asked both parents to meet me and the principal tomorrow morning, and informed the principal today about the photo being shared.

Her missing school is a warning sign. We will not wait.

— Harsha Ma'am

qa.q: How many days had Shreya been absent?
qa.a: Two days, Monday and Tuesday.

qa.q: How did Shreya seem to feel when she came back to school?
qa.a: She seemed isolated and ashamed, sitting alone and pulling her dupatta close as others whispered and whistled.

qa.q: Why was Harsha Ma'am right not to wait?
qa.a: Shreya's missing school and her father's threat were warning signs, so acting the same day with the counsellor, principal and parents protected her.

qa.q: How might Shreya's father see the photo, and why might a meeting help?
qa.a: He may see it as a threat to the family's reputation; hearing from the teacher that Shreya did nothing wrong could ease his anger.

grounding: A teacher's note shows Shreya stared at and whispered about after a rumour, facing family pressure and skipping school, and the teacher acting the same day.

passage:
Thursday

I didn't go to school today either. Third day.

Everyone thinks Yash and I are "together" because someone posted a photo of us at the bus stop. We were just waiting for the same bus. Now boys shout his name when I walk past. Girls I thought were my friends stopped sitting with me.

Abbu saw the photo. He didn't shout. It was worse. He said, "People are talking. Maybe you should stay home for a while." Ammi looked at the floor.

I feel like the whole town is looking at me through the walls.

Then this evening Khala came. She heard from Ammi. She sat on my bed, read everything, and said, "You've done nothing wrong, Afreen." Then she called my class teacher, right there, and made Abbu sit with her while she talked. Ma'am said to come tomorrow; she'll meet me at the gate.

I think I'll go.

qa.q: How many days had Afreen missed school?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: How does Afreen feel after the photo spreads?
qa.a: She feels isolated, ashamed and watched, as if the whole town is looking at her through the walls.

qa.q: What did Khala do that helped, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She told Afreen she'd done nothing wrong and called the class teacher that same evening, with Abbu present, so Afreen had support to return to school.

qa.q: What might Abbu be feeling when he says "People are talking"?
qa.a: He may be worried about the family's reputation and anxious about gossip, more than angry at Afreen.

grounding: Afreen's diary shows her isolated by a rumour, pressured by family and skipping school, until her aunt acts the same evening with her teacher.

passage: In Bhadrachalam, the rumour reached Shreya's house before she did: that she had been seen alone with Kishore from the next street behind the temple fair. She had only asked him the time. At school, boys hummed film songs when she passed, and girls she'd known since Class 1 moved their bags so she couldn't sit. At home Chachi said, "People are talking. A girl must think of the family's name," and Chacha suggested she stay home "for a few days, until it settles." Shreya didn't argue. For three days she lay facing the wall. On the third afternoon her maths teacher, Mr Varghese, came to the house. He sat with her parents on the verandah and said, "Shreya has done nothing wrong. Staying away is a warning sign, not a solution. Let's meet the headmistress tomorrow morning, together." Listening from the doorway, Shreya breathed out properly for the first time in days.

qa.q: What had Shreya actually done at the temple fair?
qa.a: She had only asked Kishore the time.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling during the three days she lay facing the wall?
qa.a: She felt isolated, ashamed and hopeless after the stares, the humming and the pressure at home, even though she had done nothing wrong.

qa.q: Why was Mr Varghese's visit the right step at this stage?
qa.a: He treated her staying away as a warning sign, told her family plainly she had done nothing wrong, and set up a meeting with the headmistress for the next morning.

qa.q: How might Chachi see the situation?
qa.a: Chachi seems worried about what people say and the family's name, and may not yet see how much the pressure is hurting Shreya.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl stared at and whispered about, pressured at home over reputation and staying away from school, and an adult treating that as a warning to act.
